newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Ratings agencies scotch NZ's hopes of Triple A.
newsitem.headline: Ratings agencies scotch NZ's hopes of Triple A.

text.p: Ratings agencies Standard and Poor's and Moody's on Tuesday scotched New Zealand's hopes of an imminent return to the Triple A sovereign credit pedestal.
Both agencies, due to visit New Zealand shortly, told Reuters their present ratings were stable and unlikley to change, despite the ministrations of the country's treasurer.
"We don't actually consider that there's anything new and startling that we haven't taken into account," S&P Sovereign Risk Management Director David Beers said from New York.
S&P and Moody's upgraded New Zealand's sovereign credit rating to AA+ and Aa1 respectively in early 1996.

New Zealand's coalition government, boasting budget surpluses and low inflation, believes the country has never been more deserving of a ratings upgrade to the elusive Triple A, lost in 1983 during the reign of Prime Minister Robert Muldoon.
New Zealand dropped three steps down the ratings ladder during a traumatic economic readjustment in the 1980s and early 1990s, but has recouped two steps as the reforms took effect.

"New Zealand's chances of achieving a return to a Triple A credit rating are higher than ever," Finance Minister Bill Birch said last week. His comments were reinforced by Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters, who said New Zealand deserved a Triple A rating.
"We are deserving of one. When the two institutions Standard and Poor's and Moody's come visiting...we have got some good news to tell them," Peters told Reuters in a interview.
"I expect their assessment to reflect the reality of an economy which is being soundly managed with healthy surpluses (and) a slightly slower debt repayment schedule."
But the ratings agencies were quick to point out a visit to New Zealand did not necessarily portend any ratings action.

"We know what's happening in New Zealand. Our rating changes are not key to the timing of our visits. When we last upgraded New Zealand in early '96, that wasn't because we rushed over there minutes before," Beers said.
Yves LeMay, Moody's analyst in charge of New Zealand, said there was "strong stability" in the country's present rating, which already took account of economic reforms of the past decade.

"Our view is that much of the progress that we've seen through the very extensive reform programmes implemented in the last 10 years are reflected in the ratings actions that we've taken in the last few years," he said from New York.
Beers agreed.

"People should understand that when we upgraded the sovereign (rating) last time, it was based upon a view of the likely evolution of fiscal policy, and some other things that we follow, which we think has broadly evolved in line with our expectations," he said.

"There's nothing particularly that is happening now which is suggesting to us that the fiscal position, for example, is any more robust than we considered it to be. And of course at the time of the upgrade, the forward looking projections out of the (New Zealand) Treasury were much higher than they are today."

In March, Treasury projected a NZ$3.3 billion surplus for 1997/98, falling to $2.6 billion in 1998/99 before rising to $3.5 billion in 1999/2000. It had previously forecast a $4.4 billion surplus for 1998/99 and $6.1 billion for 1999/2000.
Beers said the confidence that the treasurer and finance minister had expressed in obtaining a ratings upgrade was typical of their political station.

"The minister and his predecessors obviously are interested in getting the highest rating that they can for the sovereign, and we understand that -- they're certainly not unique in that regard," he said.
